titre: Gideon v. Wainwright, the lawyer a pencil petition won
accroche: In 1962, an inmate writes in pencil, on prison paper, to demand the lawyer he was refused. The Supreme Court rules in his favor in 1963, unanimously.
contenu_vulgarise:
On January 5, 1962, Clarence Earl Gideon writes out, in pencil, on lined paper supplied by the Florida prison where he is held, a petition addressed to the Supreme Court of the United States. He presents himself as a pauper and states that he was unconstitutionally denied the right to a lawyer at his trial for breaking into a pool hall. He was sentenced to five years in prison after defending himself: Florida law provided for a court-appointed lawyer only in capital offenses.

## A right that stopped at the state line

The Sixth Amendment to the United States Constitution guarantees, in every criminal prosecution, the accused's right to the assistance of counsel. For federal courts, the Supreme Court had already held that this right extended to people without means, unless validly waived. But in 1942, in *Betts v. Brady*, the Court refused to extend this obligation to state courts, reasoning that the absence of a lawyer did not, in itself, make a trial unfair. Twenty years later, it is this precedent that Gideon's petition, written from his cell, calls into question.

The Court agrees to hear the case and appoints Abe Fortas, a well-known Washington lawyer who will himself become a Supreme Court justice a few years later, to represent him. The case is argued on January 15, 1963. On March 18, the Supreme Court rules unanimously, nine votes to none: *Betts v. Brady* must be overruled. The opinion, written by Justice Hugo Black, takes up the very words of the 1942 decision to reverse its conclusion: the right to counsel is "fundamental and essential to a fair trial." From then on, protected by the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, this right applies to the states as well, and not only to federal courts.

## What a sheet of ruled paper changes

*Gideon v. Wainwright*, 372 U.S. 335 (1963), is made possible by a document that no one other than its author had any reason to take seriously: a handwritten petition, written without legal training, by a man who had neither the means nor, until then, the right to be represented. The Supreme Court of the United States treated it as a request for review (*writ of certiorari*) and accepted it. Gideon gets a second trial, this time with a lawyer. He is acquitted.

The original petition, kept at the U.S. National Archives and now on display in Washington, settles nothing by itself: a handwritten document on prison paper has no legal authority of its own. What changed American law was not the petition but the Court's decision to read it through rather than set it aside. Between the hand that writes in pencil and the hand that signs the ruling, there is no link of necessity: only nine justices who chose not to stop at the form of the document and to examine its substance.

citation.texte: Upon full reconsideration we conclude that Betts v. Brady should be overruled.
citation.auteur: Justice Hugo Black, opinion of the Court

carte.punch: In 1962, an inmate writes in pencil to demand the lawyer he was refused.
carte.idee: In 1962, Clarence Earl Gideon writes a handwritten petition to the Supreme Court from his cell. In 1963, the Court rules unanimously that states must provide a lawyer to indigent defendants, overturning twenty years of contrary precedent. Retried with a lawyer, Gideon is acquitted.

quiz.question: What does the Supreme Court of the United States rule in Gideon v. Wainwright (1963)?
choix: The right to a lawyer for indigent defendants also applies to state courts, not only to federal courts
Only capital offenses entitle a defendant to a court-appointed lawyer in every state
Handwritten petitions can no longer be considered by the Supreme Court
Betts v. Brady (1942) remains applicable, but only in Florida
quiz.explication: The Court rules unanimously that the right to counsel, guaranteed by the Sixth Amendment, is protected against the states by the Fourteenth Amendment, and overrules Betts v. Brady (1942). Florida's law, which limited court-appointed lawyers to capital offenses, is precisely what the ruling strikes down; handwritten petitions remain admissible, and it is in fact through one that the case began.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What had the Supreme Court decided in Betts v. Brady (1942), which Gideon v. Wainwright overturns twenty years later?
choix: The absence of a lawyer in a state trial does not, in itself, make that trial unfair
No defendant, even a federal one, has a right to a court-appointed lawyer
Only lawyers approved by the Supreme Court may argue criminal cases
States may not try any criminal case without the consent of a federal judge
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Betts v. Brady (1942) held that the absence of a lawyer did not, in itself, make a state trial unfair, leaving states free not to provide one outside capital offenses. The ruling did not deny the right to counsel in federal courts, did not reserve advocacy to lawyers approved by the Supreme Court, and did not make state trials subject to a federal judge's consent.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Whom does the Supreme Court appoint to defend Clarence Earl Gideon before it?
choix: Abe Fortas, a Washington lawyer who will himself become a Supreme Court justice
Hugo Black, the justice who will later write the opinion of the Court
A Florida lawyer, appointed by the state prosecuting Gideon
No one: Gideon kept defending himself before the Court
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Court appoints Abe Fortas, a well-known Washington lawyer who will become a Supreme Court justice a few years later. Hugo Black is the justice who writes the opinion of the Court, not Gideon's lawyer; the State of Florida is the opposing party, and Gideon is indeed represented before the Supreme Court, unlike at his first trial.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happens to Clarence Earl Gideon after the Supreme Court's decision?
choix: He is retried with a lawyer, and he is acquitted
His original conviction is permanently overturned, with no new trial
He stays in prison: the decision applies only to future cases
He is retried but convicted a second time, with a heavier sentence
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Gideon gets a second trial, this time with a lawyer, and he is acquitted. The Supreme Court does not itself pronounce a final acquittal without a new trial, the decision applies to his own case and not only to future ones, and he is not convicted a second time.
